lead: Noise is a random signal added to the true pixel value. Its probability density p(z) tells how likely each grey level z is. The shape of p(z) matters because a filter that suits Gaussian noise may fail on salt-and-pepper noise. Engineers measure the density on a flat patch, then choose a filter. This chapter lists the standard densities, their parameters, and the physical source of each.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for where n enters the model, and Unit 2 histograms.

blocks.text: The observed pixel is g(x,y) = f(x,y) + n(x,y). f is the true grey level, n is a random noise value, and x,y are pixel coordinates. n is independent of f and changes from pixel to pixel. The same equation holds for all pixels, so we can drop coordinates and write g = f + n.
Multiplicative noise is different: g = f·n, common in radar and laser speckle. A log transform turns it into additive noise.

The noise is described by its probability density p(z). z is a grey level, and p(z)dz is the probability that n lies between z and z+dz. The mean µ = E[z] and variance σ² = E[(z−µ)²] summarise the centre and spread. A flat patch has almost constant f, so the histogram of that patch estimates p(z).
Periodic noise, such as a sine ripple from a power supply, is not random in this sense and does not fit these densities. It gets a frequency-domain treatment in 3.4.
In each row the parameters belong to that row only. For impulse noise, P_a + P_b = 1, and a and b are grey levels.

blocks.text: Unipolar impulse noise has one impulse value a and clean pixels at c: put b=c and P_b=1−P in the bipolar row. Salt-and-pepper is bipolar with a=0 and b=255 in 8-bit images.

sections.h3: Estimating parameters from a flat patch

blocks.text: Noise is measured where the true image is flat. A textured or edged region adds real variation and inflates the estimate.
µ̂ = (1/N) Σ z_i,   σ̂² = (1/N) Σ (z_i − µ̂)²
blocks.where: z_i is the i-th pixel in the patch; N is the number of pixels; µ̂ is the sample mean; σ̂² is the sample variance.

items: Pick a region with no edges or texture, at least 20×20 pixels if possible.
Plot its histogram; for a flat patch this histogram estimates p(z).
Compute the sample mean and variance with the formulas above.
Match the histogram shape: symmetric bell → Gaussian; one-sided tail with z≥a → Rayleigh or gamma; flat top → uniform; spikes at two levels → impulse.

For a Gaussian, assume zero-mean noise, estimate the flat level by µ̂, and report σ̂ as the noise standard deviation. For other densities, solve the mean and variance equations for the PDF parameters.

blocks.text: The fitted density is only a model. If the histogram has isolated spikes, treat the image as having impulse noise first; a mean filter is the wrong tool there. Filters for each density are in 3.3.

spec.aria: The 3 by 3 patch 8 10 12 / 10 12 14 / 12 14 16, a histogram with counts 1, 2, 3, 2, 1 at levels 8 to 16 and a Gaussian curve over it centred on 12 with σ marked, and a box with the steps mean 12, variance 5.33, σ 2.31.

examples.question: A flat 3×3 patch reads 8, 10, 12, 10, 12, 14, 12, 14, 16 grey levels. Estimate the mean, variance and standard deviation of these readings, and state a suitable noise density.
steps: The histogram is symmetric about 12 with no spikes, so zero-mean Gaussian noise with σ ≈ 2.31 grey levels fits this patch, whose flat true level is estimated as 12 grey levels.
A real measurement would use a patch of 20×20 pixels or more; 9 readings are used here only to keep the arithmetic short, so the estimate is rough.
examples.answer: Gaussian noise of mean µ = 0, variance 5.33 grey levels² and standard deviation 2.31 grey levels; the flat level of the patch is 12 grey levels.
examples.check:
vals=[8,10,12,10,12,14,12,14,16]
n=len(vals)
mean=sum(vals)/n
sq=[(v-mean)**2 for v in vals]
var=sum(sq)/n
sigma=var**0.5
print(round(mean,2))
print(round(var,2))
print(round(sigma,2))

traps: Reporting the variance of the whole image as the noise variance. Edges and texture inflate it; measure only on a flat patch.
Using a mean filter on impulse noise. Impulses have no useful variance, and averaging smears them instead of removing them; use an order-statistic filter from 3.3.
Confusing variance σ² with standard deviation σ. The Gaussian parameter in p(z) is σ, not σ².
Using the wrong parameterisation for Rayleigh or gamma noise. The mean is not a or b alone; check the mean and variance formulas before fitting.
Treating periodic noise as a PDF noise. A sine ripple gives spectral spikes, not a smooth histogram; use the notch filter in 3.4.

quiz.q: Write the Gaussian noise density and name its two parameters.
quiz.a: p(z) = 1/(√(2π)σ) exp(−(z−µ)²/(2σ²)). The parameters are the mean µ and the standard deviation σ; the variance is σ².

quiz.q: What are the two impulse values in 8-bit salt-and-pepper noise, and what does each look like?
quiz.a: The values are 0 (pepper, black) and 255 (salt, white). Bipolar impulse noise has probabilities P_a at one level and P_b at the other, with P_a + P_b = 1.

quiz.q: Why does quantisation produce approximately uniform noise?
quiz.a: Quantisation rounds a continuous value to the nearest level. The rounding error is roughly equally likely anywhere between −Δ/2 and +Δ/2, where Δ is the step between levels. A flat density over that interval is uniform.

quiz.q: Why is a mean filter a poor choice for impulse noise?
quiz.a: An impulse is a rare, extreme value. Its variance is not a useful measure of spread, and averaging spreads the extreme value over neighbouring pixels. A median or other order-statistic filter removes the impulse without blurring the edge.

quiz.q: Exponential noise has p(z) = a e^(−az) for z≥0, with a = 0.2 grey-level⁻¹. Find its mean and variance.
quiz.a: Mean = 1/a = 1/0.2 = 5 grey levels. Variance = 1/a² = 1/0.04 = 25 grey levels².

quiz.q: Bipolar impulse noise has P_a = 0.1 at a = 0 and P_b = 0.9 at b = 255. Find the variance.
A flat patch histogram has a broad Gaussian cluster plus isolated counts at 0 and 255. What two noise types are present, and what filter order makes sense?
quiz.a: The broad cluster is Gaussian noise; the isolated counts at 0 and 255 are bipolar impulse noise. Remove impulses first with a median or order-statistic filter, then average to reduce the Gaussian part. Averaging first would smear the impulses.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real cameras combine Gaussian read noise with Poisson shot noise, so denoisers estimate a noise level function that changes with brightness. Phone cameras and video codecs use this estimate to set thresholds before compression or night mode. Modern denoisers such as BM3D (patch matching with a fixed transform) and CNN-based learned models still start from a noise model. Search for Poisson-Gaussian noise, noise level function, and blind denoising.
